terms.gloss: acknowledge, own (as one’s own or as true)
evidence: Cic. Fam. 4.4.1: mē nōn esse verbōrum admodum inopem agnōscō
Cic. Fam. 5.20.5: id ego agnōvī meō jussū esse factum
terms.comment: Lewis & Short: to acknowledge a thing as one’s own, a deed, a debt, a child, a fault (culpam agnōscere, see accept blame); with an accusative and infinitive, to admit that.

terms.gloss: admit, confess; said in passing, “I admit”
evidence: Ter. Heaut. 158: ita rēs est, fateor
Cic. Att. 2.1.5: fateor; sed ego illam ōdī
terms.comment: Usually with an accusative and infinitive (Lewis & Short).
Lewis & Short: of owning to an error or to something denied before, at some cost to one’s will; fateor is a plain acknowledgement.

phrases.latin: et ego ipse … mē nōn esse verbōrum admodum inopem agnōscō
phrases.english: and I myself admit that I am not altogether short of words

phrases.latin: Ita rēs est, fateor: peccātum ā mē maximum est.
phrases.english: That is how it is, I admit: I have done a very great wrong.

phrases.latin: Ego mē amāre hanc fateor: sī id peccāre est, fateor id quoque.
phrases.english: I admit that I love her; if that is a sin, I admit that too.

sources: Lewis & Short: agnosco · Lewis & Short: fateor · Lewis & Short: confiteor
Cicero’s letters (Fam. 4.4.1, 5.20.5; Att. 2.1.5) and Terence (Heaut. 158, And. 896) checked against the Perseus Latin texts (9 November 2026).
Quotations marked “Lewis & Short” are given as Lewis & Short cites them, with its references, in the house spelling (macrons, consonantal j); they have not been checked against a modern edition.
